target.title: fix(plugins): bound plugin manifest metadata file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin manifest metadata scan reads `openclaw.plugin.json` files from installed, bundled, and global plugin directories through unbounded `fs.readFileSync`. A corrupted or hostile manifest file could therefore exhaust memory during metadata enumeration.

## Why This Change Was Made

Plugin manifest files are small metadata descriptors like workspace hook manifests. The shared bounded `readRegularFileSync` helper with the same 256 KiB maximum used by the full plugin manifest loader now enforces the cap during metadata scanning as well. An oversized manifest is logged and skipped; scanning continues for remaining plugins.

## User Impact

Oversized plugin manifests are warned about and skipped. Metadata scan continues for other plugins.

## Maintainer Changes

- Added `PLUGIN_MANIFEST_METADATA_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024` constant, matching the existing limit in the full plugin manifest loader (`src/plugins/manifest.ts` `MAX_PLUGIN_MANIFEST_BYTES`).
- Replaced unbounded `fs.readFileSync` with `readRegularFileSync` bounded reader.
- Handles oversized files via `readRegularFileSync` error (plain `Error` with "exceeds" message): logs a subsystem warning and returns `undefined` so the oversized plugin is skipped.
- Added two bounding coverage tests: oversized manifest skipped, exact-limit manifest accepted.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof: bounded manifest read via listOpenClawPluginManifestMetadata

The bounded reader correctly handles all three cases — normal, oversized, and exact-limit manifests — against the **real** discovered plugin tree including source checkout, bundled, and global plugin paths. The run uses a fresh OPENCLAW_HOME with no SQLite state DB, so `readPersistedInstalledPluginIndexSync` returns null (bypasses the SQLite WAL-safety check entirely).

**Subsystem warning output (stderr):**

```
[WARN] [plugins/manifest-metadata-scan] Ignoring oversized plugin manifest at /tmp/.../big-plugin/openclaw.plugin.json: file exceeds the 262144-byte limit
```

**Scan results:**

```
── Test data ──
Good manifest size:    51 bytes
Oversized manifest:    262145 bytes (> 256 KiB)
Exact manifest size:   262144 bytes (== 256 KiB)

── Scan results ──
Total plugins discovered:  150
good-plugin found:          true
big-plugin (oversized):     false (expected: false — skipped)
exact-plugin (256 KiB):     true (expected: true — accepted)

── Verification ──
  ✅ Oversized manifest skipped
  ✅ Valid plugin still discovered
  ✅ Exact-limit manifest accepted
  ✅ Subsystem warning emitted

ALL CHECKS PASSED
```

The 150 discovered plugins include all bundled extensions and the test good-plugin, confirming that manifest discovery continues normally after the oversized entry is skipped.

target.title: fix: prevent parallel talk tests from sharing SQLite state
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where parallel OpenClaw checkouts on the same machine could share the real `/tmp/openclaw-agent.sqlite` database while running `src/talk/agent-consult-runtime.test.ts`. A newer checkout could advance that database to schema version 11, causing an older checkout that supports schema version 10 to fail.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each test now gets a `realpath`-canonicalized `mkdtemp` directory, and every mocked agent, workspace, session, and store path derives from it. Teardown closes the exact cached agent database before recursively removing the directory. A sibling-test scan found no other hardcoded `/tmp` paths under `src/talk`.

## User Impact

No runtime behavior changes. Maintainers and contributors can run talk tests from parallel worktrees without cross-checkout SQLite schema contamination.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/talk` — 37 files passed, 219 tests passed on the final rebased head.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` — core test typecheck, changed-file lint, formatting, temp-directory guard, and boundary checks passed on [Blacksmith Testbox](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29595365269).
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode uncommitted` — clean; no accepted or actionable findings.
- `rg` scan — no hardcoded `/tmp` paths remain in `src/talk` test/spec files.

AI-assisted with Codex. I reviewed the implementation and validation results.

target.title: fix(feishu): log message content JSON parse failures instead of silently swallowing
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves `parseFeishuMessageContent` used an empty `catch {}` that silently swallowed `JSON.parse` failures. The prior fix added `formatErrorMessage(err)` to the log, but V8 `JSON.parse` error messages can include the malformed input content — risking message content leakage in verbose logs. ## Why This Change Was Made **Security:** `formatErrorMessage(err)` performs pattern-based redaction only, and does not guarantee removal of arbitrary user message content from V8 error messages. A malformed Feishu message body could leak to operator logs. The fix replaces the exception-derived log text with safe metadata (message type, message ID) while preserving the raw-content fallback. ## User Impact - **Before (empty catch):** Bad JSON parse errors were invisible to operators. - **Before (formatErrorMessage):** Error text could leak message content through V8 JSON.parse error messages. - **After:** Verbose/debug logging records only safe metadata — `feishu message content parse failed for text message (id: om_xxx)` — never the exception message or raw content. target.title: fix(cron): prevent double dispatch after disable/enable cycle during in-flight run
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Disabling and re-enabling a cron job while a run is still in flight cleared the persisted `runningAtMs` reservation. The next scheduler tick then saw a past-due `nextRunAtMs` with no concurrency guard and dispatched a second overlapping run.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three cooperating owners keep the in-flight guard intact:

1. `finalizeUpdatedJob` — on disable, keep `runningAtMs` **only while** `isCronJobActive(job.id)` so queued force reservations can still clear and be replaced (same-millisecond admission).
2. `normalizeJobTickState` — for disabled jobs, clear `runningAtMs` only when stuck **and** not a queued force reservation (`isQueuedForceCronRun`).
3. `isRunnableJob` — also reject when `isCronJobActive(job.id)`.

## User Impact

Operators who disable/re-enable a job during an active run no longer get a second concurrent execution of that job. Force re-run after disable (queued admission) keeps working.

## Evidence

| Layer | Proof |
| --- | --- |
| Head | `29f692e794f6110ea6d982a02ffe7fb310a6e945` (on `main` tip rebuild + CI fix) |
| Scope | 4 files, +83 / −7 |
| L1 | `ops.regression.test.ts` `#102238` — mid-run disable→enable→`onTimer` stays single dispatch |
| L1 sibling | `ops.run-admission` same-ms replacement after disable must keep working (CI regression that failed when disable always preserved `runningAtMs`) |
| CI fix | Preserve `runningAtMs` on disable only if `isCronJobActive`; oxfmt on touched files |

Fixes #102238

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where message actions that pass channel-specific `channelData` as a JSON string could lose that payload or fail to treat it as send content when the visible text is blank or removed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The message tool, outbound runner, and embedded subscribe rich-content tracker now parse `channelData` with the same structured JSON boundary used for sibling message payload fields. Opaque `channelData` remains fail-closed when it contains protected internal runtime context, while ordinary visible text keeps the safe text that remains after protected context is stripped. The runner now counts valid object-shaped `channelData` as real send content without adding config, schema, provider, or compatibility behavior.

target.title: fix(google-oauth): cancel unread response body on non-ok HTTP responses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two response body leaks in Google OAuth project operations where HTTP error responses with unread bodies could keep the connection open until idle timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

When the polling loop or onboardUser endpoint returns a non-ok HTTP status, the response body stream is not consumed before continuing or throwing. Unread response bodies can delay connection reuse and, in resource-constrained environments, contribute to file descriptor pressure.

The fix adds `response.body?.cancel()` before each `continue` and `throw`, matching the established pattern used across the codebase (openrouter/usage.ts, chutes/oauth.ts, lmstudio/models.fetch.ts, and others).

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. Connection reuse is slightly more efficient during Google OAuth project polling.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local development environment

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `npx tsx scripts/evidence-oauth.ts` — direct call to the `pollOperation`/`discoverProject` error path

**After-fix evidence**:
```
  [RUN] Body cancel on non-ok response... Body cancelled: YES ✅ PASS ✅
  [RUN] Double cancel is safe... Double cancel count: 2 — safe ✅ PASS ✅
  [RUN] Null body is handled gracefully... Null body cancel: No error ✅ PASS ✅
  [RUN] Cancel rejection doesn't mask original error... Cancel rejection: Suppressed by .catch ✅
        Final error: "Original error (status 401)"
        Original error preserved: YES ✅ PASS ✅

Results: 4/4 passed
COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0
```

**Observed result after the fix**:
- `response.body?.cancel()` executes before throwing on non-ok responses
- Double cancel is safe
- Null body is handled gracefully
- Cancel rejection doesn't mask the original error
- Original error is preserved with correct status code

**What was not tested**: Full Gateway integration with real Google OAuth. The above evidence covers the response body cancellation pattern that was added.

target.title: fix(transcripts): imported text can inject terminal escapes through transcripts show
target.body:
Closes #102392

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators viewing a stored transcript summary with `openclaw transcripts show` would have raw terminal control sequences replayed into their terminal when the imported transcript text contained escape bytes. A transcript line such as `ESC[2J ESC[31mADMIN APPROVED ESC[0m` could clear the screen, spoof colored status text, or emit other terminal controls the moment the summary was displayed, because the escape bytes were persisted verbatim into `summary.md` and written directly to stdout. `transcripts list` had the same sink: session titles and externally supplied session IDs were formatted into list lines unsanitized.

## Why This Change Was Made

Sanitization is applied at presentation boundaries only; canonical identity is never rewritten. `summarizeTranscripts` sanitizes the derived summary content (utterance text, speaker labels, session title) with the existing terminal-core `sanitizeTerminalText` helper, `renderTranscriptsMarkdown` sanitizes the session ID it renders into the `Session:` line, `transcripts show` sanitizes stored markdown line by line at the stdout boundary so summaries persisted before this change are also protected, and `transcripts list` sanitizes the metadata columns it prints.

`TranscriptsSummary.sessionId` keeps the raw provider-supplied session ID. `TranscriptsStore.writeSummary` uses that field to locate the existing metadata and transcript directory when the optional session descriptor is not passed, so a lossy rewrite would misplace regenerated summary artifacts under a different directory. Identity stays raw; only rendering sanitizes.

The selector printed by `transcripts list` is now the directory-backed form `YYYY-MM-DD/<safe-segment>`, the same conservative segment the store uses on disk. It is terminal-safe by construction (no control bytes can survive `safeSegment`), and `show` and `path` resolve that exact printed value in addition to the raw session ID, so the documented copy-the-selector workflow keeps working for externally supplied IDs that carry escape bytes. For ordinary session IDs the printed selector is byte-identical to before.

The raw capture in `transcript.jsonl` and the stored `metadata.json`/`summary.json` are intentionally left untouched for fidelity; they are JSON-encoded on disk, so control bytes are escaped, and the CLI JSON output paths escape them via `JSON.stringify` as well.

## User Impact

Operators can view summaries of imported or captured transcripts and list stored sessions without untrusted transcript content executing terminal control sequences in their terminal. Selectors printed by `transcripts list` can always be copied back into `transcripts show` and `transcripts path`, including for session IDs containing escape bytes. Summary artifacts regenerated without a session descriptor keep landing in the original session directory. Plain transcript content and plain session IDs render exactly as before.

## Evidence

Live before/after on the real transcripts pipeline: a hostile transcript is imported through the real manual transcript provider, persisted through the real `TranscriptsStore` (summary written without the optional session descriptor), then driven through the real `transcripts list`, `show`, and `path` commands, on identical inputs. Only `src/transcripts/summary.ts` and `src/cli/program/register.transcripts.ts` are switched between pristine `main` (4a675228af) and this patch (head 7ee6df2a21). Escape bytes are shown in `cat -v` form (`^[` is the raw ESC byte); the selector passed to `show` and `path` is copied programmatically from the first column of `list` output.

```
=== BEFORE (pristine main 4a675228af) ===
--- seed: real import -> TranscriptsStore -> writeSummary (no session descriptor) ---
{"summaryWrittenTo":".../transcripts/2026-07-16/ansi--31mprovider-0m/summary.md","summaryInOriginalDir":true}
--- openclaw transcripts list ---
2026-07-16/ansi-^[[31mprovider^[[0m	2026-07-16T10:00:00.000Z	^[[31mQ3 Board sync^[[0m	.../summary.md
--- openclaw transcripts show <selector copied from list> ---
# ^[[31mQ3 Board sync^[[0m
...
Session: ansi-^[[31mprovider^[[0m
## Overview
^[[2J^[[31mADMIN APPROVED^[[0m decision: ship it
...
rawEscapeByteLinesInList=1 rawEscapeByteLinesInShow=6

=== AFTER (this patch, identical inputs, head 7ee6df2a21) ===
--- seed: real import -> TranscriptsStore -> writeSummary (no session descriptor) ---
{"summaryWrittenTo":".../transcripts/2026-07-16/ansi--31mprovider-0m/summary.md","summaryInOriginalDir":true}
--- openclaw transcripts list ---
2026-07-16/ansi--31mprovider-0m	2026-07-16T10:00:00.000Z	Q3 Board sync	.../summary.md
--- copied selector from list: 2026-07-16/ansi--31mprovider-0m ---
--- openclaw transcripts show <selector> ---
# Q3 Board sync
...
Session: ansi-provider
## Overview
ADMIN APPROVED decision: ship it
...
--- openclaw transcripts path <selector> ---
.../transcripts/2026-07-16/ansi--31mprovider-0m/summary.md
rawEscapeByteLinesInList=0 rawEscapeByteLinesInShow=0
```

Before the patch, `list` and `show` replay the raw ESC bytes (screen clear `^[[2J` plus color spoofing) into the terminal. After the patch, no escape byte reaches the terminal, the summary written without a descriptor still lands in the original session directory with its raw `sessionId` preserved in `summary.json`, and the selector printed by `list` resolves through both `show` and `path`.

Regression coverage: `src/transcripts/summary.test.ts` proves CSI, OSC 8, and C1 CSI sequences are stripped from rendered content while `summary.sessionId` keeps the raw provider ID and the rendered `Session:` line is sanitized; `src/transcripts/store.test.ts` proves `writeSummary` without a session descriptor stores the summary in the existing session directory for an ANSI-bearing session ID; `src/cli/program/register.transcripts.test.ts` drives import through the manual provider and store, asserts `show` and `list` output carry no ESC bytes, covers legacy summaries at the `show` boundary, and round-trips the printed `list` selector through `show` and `path`.

Local gates on the changed files: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/transcripts/summary.test.ts src/transcripts/store.test.ts src/cli/program/register.transcripts.test.ts src/agents/tools/transcripts-tool.test.ts` (35 passed on the rebased head), `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` clean on the changed files, `git diff --check` clean.

target.title: fix(feishu): lock timeoutMs preflight abort for stalled DNS lookup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Feishu app registration can hang when SSRF DNS/proxy preflight never completes. Without an entry-point regression on `beginAppRegistration`, a future change can stop forwarding `timeoutMs` into `fetchWithSsrFGuard` and leave onboarding stuck before HTTP dispatch.

## Why This Change Was Made

Current `main` (after [#105549](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/105549)) owns registration deadlines via **guard top-level `timeoutMs`**, not `AbortSignal.timeout()` in `RequestInit`. `beginAppRegistration(domain, options?)` still accepts test-only `fetchImpl` / `lookupFn` / `timeoutMs`.

This PR is test-only: it locks that contract for a never-resolving `lookupFn`, asserting `TimeoutError` + `message: "request timed out"` and that `fetchImpl` is never called. Shared SSRF suite already covers stalled DNS at the guard; this covers the Feishu registration wiring into that owner.

Rebuilt onto latest `main` `c69a75f697876c6e0b75996f10306b3ca6467203`.

AI-assisted: yes. I inspected current `fetchFeishuJson` / `beginAppRegistration`, #105549, sibling hang-without-headers coverage, and `fetch-guard.ssrf` stalled-DNS tests before updating.

## User Impact

No runtime change. CI keeps a focused lock that stalled Feishu registration preflight fails closed with the guard-owned diagnostic and without opening an HTTP request.

## Evidence

**Contract on current main** (`extensions/feishu/src/app-registration.ts`): `fetchWithSsrFGuard({ ..., timeoutMs })` — see #105549 (“a second AbortSignal.timeout path was redundant”).

**Focused suite:** `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/feishu/src/app-registration.test.ts` → **11 passed**

**Refreshed entry-point proof** (production `beginAppRegistration`, no Vitest):

```text
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 80ms (elapsed 81ms) operation=fetchWithSsrFGuard url=https://accounts.feishu.cn/oauth/v1/app/registration
```

```json
{
  "phase": "beginAppRegistration-stalled-lookup",
  "mainContract": "timeoutMs → fetchWithSsrFGuard (#105549)",
  "timed_out": true,
  "name": "TimeoutError",
  "message": "request timed out",
  "elapsed_ms": 192
}
```

```text
[feishu preflight stall proof] timed_out=true name=TimeoutError message=request timed out elapsed_ms=81 fetch_called=0
```

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(telegram): duplicate inbound messages after a transient update-offset persistence failure
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Telegram users on a self-hosted OpenClaw gateway can have
already-handled inbound messages re-delivered and re-processed after a restart,
producing duplicate replies and duplicate side effects (re-run tools/commands).

The trigger is a *transient* failure while persisting the Telegram Bot API
update offset (the durable watermark the gateway saves so it can resume without
replaying old updates). Any temporary hiccup in the plugin state store (disk I/O
error, lock contention, quota) makes the offset write fail. When that happens
the gateway logs the error but never catches the offset back up, so the durable
offset silently drifts behind the position the gateway has actually processed.
On the next restart the bot resumes from that stale offset and Telegram
re-delivers everything after it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The update tracker coalesces offset writes behind a single in-flight write and a
monotonic "highest requested" high-water mark. Previously, when a write threw,
`drainPersistQueue` only reported the error: it dropped the pending target and
left the request high-water mark advanced, so (1) the failed offset was never
retried and (2) a later request for the same offset was short-circuited by the
`updateId <= highestPersistenceRequestedUpdateId` guard. The durable offset
could then only ever move again if some strictly higher offset happened to
persist successfully.

This change makes offset persistence resilient to transient failures without
touching the coalescing fast path or any public API:

- On a failed write it keeps the durable watermark unchanged (unchanged
  behavior), re-arms the failed offset (unless a newer coalesced target already
  supersedes it), and rolls the request high-water mark back to the durable
  floor so the same offset can be requested and retried.
- It retries on a bounded exponential backoff (250ms up to 5s, `unref`ed) so a
  temporary storage outage recovers even on an idle chat, while a persistently
  failing writer cannot hot-spin the event loop.
- On success it resets the backoff.

The safe-completed watermark still fences the offset behind any pending or
failed update, so a retry never advances the offset past an update that is still
in flight.

### Follow-up: tie the retry to the bot lifecycle (addresses ClawSweeper review)

The first revision left the retry timer detached from the owning bot. Telegram
account removal and token changes deliberately delete the persisted offset, and
`bot.stop()` did not dispose the tracker — so a queued retry from a retired
tracker could wake after shutdown and write an already-retired offset back into
the shared account store, creating a *second* stale-offset path.

This revision gives the retry explicit lifecycle ownership:

- `createTelegramUpdateTracker` now exposes `dispose()`, which clears the pending
  retry timer and latches a `disposed` flag so no scheduled or future write can
  persist afterwards.
- `dispose()` is awaitable and fences the write that is already in flight: it
  awaits the active drain before resolving, so an offset write already dispatched
  to the store settles before shutdown completes.
- `bot-core.ts` `await`s `updateTracker.dispose()` from the existing `bot.stop`
  hook (alongside the thread-binding and outbound-recorder teardown), so offset
  cleanup on account removal / token change is sequenced strictly after any
  started write, closing the stop/delete race.
- `drainPersistQueue` also yields to disposal if it races an in-flight write, so
  it never re-arms a retry for an offset that is being retired on purpose.

## User Impact

Telegram channels no longer re-deliver and re-answer already-processed messages
after a gateway restart that followed a transient state-store error. Operators
get an offset that reliably catches up to the processed position once the
underlying storage recovers, instead of a watermark that stays stuck until new,
higher-numbered traffic arrives.

## Evidence

Added focused regression tests in
`extensions/telegram/src/bot-update-tracker.test.ts` and validated the full
tracker suite plus the closest offset/persistence integration tests.

- `vitest run extensions/telegram/src/bot-update-tracker.test.ts` -> **19 passed
  (19)** (13 existing + 6 new).
- `vitest run extensions/telegram/src/bot.create-telegram-bot.test.ts` -> **119
  passed** (covers the wrapped `bot.stop` shutdown path).
- Before/after proof: temporarily reverting the retry fix makes
  `retries a transient offset persistence failure until it succeeds` and
  `keeps retrying offset persistence across repeated transient failures` report
  `expected "vi.fn()" to be called 2 times, but got 1 times`; reverting the
  `dispose()` wiring makes `cancels a scheduled offset-persistence retry once
  disposed` fail with the retry firing after shutdown; reverting the in-flight
  fence makes `fences an in-flight persistence write before disposal resolves`
  fail because disposal resolves before the started write settles. With the fix,
  all 19 pass.
- `oxlint` on all changed files -> clean.

New tests:

1. `retries a transient offset persistence failure until it succeeds` -- one
   transient failure; the durable offset does not advance, the error is
   surfaced, and a timer-driven retry (no new traffic) persists the offset.
2. `keeps retrying offset persistence across repeated transient failures` --
   three consecutive failures back off and eventually succeed.
3. `does not persist a higher offset past an id whose write is still failing` --
   with a later update still pending, retries land the offset exactly on the
   safe id and never jump past the unfinished update.
4. `cancels a scheduled offset-persistence retry once disposed` -- after a failed
   write schedules a retry, `dispose()` clears the timer and no further write
   happens even after the backoff window elapses (stop/reconfiguration race).
5. `ignores new offset-persistence requests after being disposed` -- a disposed
   tracker does not resurrect persistence for freshly handled updates.
6. `fences an in-flight persistence write before disposal resolves` -- with a
   write already dispatched to the store, `dispose()` does not resolve until that
   write settles, so bot shutdown sequences offset cleanup strictly after it.

### Note on real-behavior proof

I don't have access to a live Telegram bot token or an outbound Telegram network
path in this environment, so I can't attach redacted live-gateway logs of an
induced store failure + restart. The behavior is instead pinned deterministically
at the exact seam the bug lives in -- the update tracker's persistence queue and
lifecycle -- covering the induced-transient-failure -> retry -> success path, the
stop/reconfiguration race, and the in-flight-write shutdown fence. Happy to add a
live-run artifact if a maintainer can point me at a fixture/harness.

target.title: fix(parallel): reject invalid search counts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users selecting Parallel web search providers could pass malformed or out-of-range `count` values and still have the provider request proceed after local coercion or clamping.

## Why This Change Was Made

The paid Parallel REST provider and the free Parallel Search MCP provider now use the same strict positive-integer count validation at their tool boundary before building provider requests. This keeps the existing default/configured `maxResults` fallback and final 1-40 normalization while rejecting caller-supplied `count` values that do not match the advertised schema.

## User Impact

Parallel web search calls now fail fast with a clear count validation error for fractional, malformed string, or over-limit result counts instead of silently sending a different `max_results` value upstream.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: paid `parallel` and free `parallel-free` web search tools reject fractional, malformed-string, and over-limit `count` values before provider transport, while valid/default count behavior still works.
- Current-head GitHub proof at `dce41e646bbcf4182680e0479f76624705fd7c61`: `Real behavior proof` passed, `checks-node-changed` passed, `check-test-types` passed, and `openclaw/ci-gate` passed.
- Current-head real-behavior proof check: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29594021999/job/87929889827 passed.
- Current-head CI gate: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29594023311/job/87930929069 passed.
- Current-head branch diff hygiene: `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passed.
- Duplicate search: open PR and issue searches for `parallel count max_results web_search` returned no overlapping results.

target.title: fix: avoid false stayed-stopped on launchd KeepAlive throttle
target.body:
Closes #109941

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running `openclaw gateway restart` on macOS would see a definitive false failure (`service stayed stopped and health checks never came up`) while a LaunchAgent-supervised gateway with `KeepAlive` was still inside launchd's normal `ThrottleInterval` respawn window and would become healthy seconds later. Automation that trusted that verdict could escalate against a recovering service.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restart health now prepares launchd KeepAlive supervision facts once before the poll loop and extends the continuous stopped-and-port-free early-exit threshold past the product `ThrottleInterval` when a loaded LaunchAgent is present. Unloaded, unmanaged, non-macOS, and non-KeepAlive paths keep the baseline fast-fail threshold. No new config knobs; supervisor facts are not rediscovered on every poll.

Compatibility: no config/API change; optional prepared `supervisor` param only. Performance: one `isLoaded` prepare at wait start. Usability: false failure verdict avoided during normal KeepAlive recovery. Security: no auth/trust change.

## User Impact

On macOS managed LaunchAgent installs, `openclaw gateway restart` no longer reports a hard "stayed stopped" failure solely because launchd is throttling a KeepAlive respawn. Genuine permanent stop / unload still fails within the existing overall restart health budget.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-wait.test.ts
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-wait.test.ts (16 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts (27 tests)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/daemon/launchd.test.ts -t "KeepAlive=true policy"
 ✓ |daemon| src/daemon/launchd.test.ts (1 test matched; product ThrottleInterval from constant)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/lifecycle.test.ts
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts (27 tests)
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/lifecycle.test.ts (34 tests)
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  61 passed (61)

$ pnpm check:changed
[check:changed] lanes=core, coreTests
… typecheck core / core tests / lint on touched files …
check:changed exit=0
```

Key new cases:

- KeepAlive + ThrottleInterval=10s early-exits only after ~20s continuous stopped+free (not the previous ~12.5s baseline false window)
- KeepAlive recovery that binds after the old 12.5s window returns `healthy` instead of `stopped-free`
- Unloaded / non-KeepAlive still uses the baseline ~12.5s early exit

## Real behavior proof

Verification host: local macOS with an isolated real LaunchAgent. The active `ai.openclaw.gateway` service was not touched.

The proof used the production LaunchAgent installer, service adapter, port inspection, and `waitForGatewayHealthyRestart` path with a random temporary label, HOME, and port. The supervised child deliberately exited on launches 1 and 2, then bound its port on launch 3. Cleanup booted out the temporary job and removed its files.

```json
{
  "proof": "isolated-real-launchd-keepalive",
  "label": "<isolated-label>",
  "keepAlive": true,
  "throttleIntervalSeconds": 10,
  "attemptsObserved": 3,
  "respawnGapsMs": [10113, 10113],
  "waitOutcome": "healthy",
  "healthy": true,
  "runtimeStatus": "running",
  "portStatus": "busy",
  "elapsedMs": 20667.57,
  "exceededOldStoppedFreeWindow": true
}
```

This exercises real launchd KeepAlive/throttle cadence: recovery occurred after the old ~12.5s stopped-free verdict window, and the patched wait returned healthy. During proof hardening, the threshold was also corrected to sample one full poll after the throttle boundary (20.5s at 500ms), rather than exactly on it.

Focused validation after the proof hardening:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-wait.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/lifecycle.test.ts
Test Files  3 passed (3)
Tests       77 passed (77)
```


## Main throttle reconciliation

Merged current `main` (`4a675228af`) into this branch. Product LaunchAgent `ThrottleInterval` on both current main and the ClawSweeper review base (`b319493a529c`) is still **10 seconds** (`LAUNCH_AGENT_THROTTLE_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 10` in `src/daemon/launchd-plist.ts`). This branch does not restore a longer default; it only exports that same product constant so restart-health can reuse it.

KeepAlive stopped-free wait tests now derive expected elapsed time from that product constant (still 10s → 20.5s early-exit at 500ms polls). The prior isolated LaunchAgent live proof remains valid for main's current 10s product throttle; a 1s throttle is not present on main, so the extra supervisor-aware tolerance is still required for KeepAlive recovery after the baseline ~12.5s stopped-free window.

## AI disclosure

This PR was authored with AI assistance (Grok).

target.title: fix(discord): submit plugin interaction text
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where external plugins could render and handle Discord callback buttons but could not submit a generic selected reply back into the originating agent conversation. This prevented channel-neutral quick-reply plugins from supporting Discord safely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds `submitText` to the shared interactive-handler result contract and maps handled, authorized Discord submissions through the existing component inbound path. The submitted text retains the source component's session, agent, account, message, channel, thread, and reply context; declined, unauthorized, empty, malformed, failed, stale, and duplicate interactions do not submit it.

Telegram now uses the same canonical result type while retaining its existing transport behavior.

## User Impact

External plugins can implement generic Discord quick-reply buttons without creating detached agent turns or hard-coding product-specific callback behavior in core.

## Evidence

- Plugin interactive tests: 17 passed
- Discord component interaction tests: 33 passed
- Plugin SDK surface check passed
- Formatting and `git diff --check` passed
- Fresh autoreview reported no actionable findings

target.title: fix(plugins): hide bundle commands when frontmatter uses on
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users shipping bundled Claude commands could set `disable-model-invocation: on` in command frontmatter and still have that command remain available for model invocation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bundle command loader now reuses the shared frontmatter boolean parser instead of maintaining a narrower local parser. This keeps the owner-local command-loading path aligned with the existing frontmatter contract without adding config, compatibility aliases, or broader plugin behavior changes.

## User Impact

Bundle authors can use common boolean frontmatter values consistently: `on`, `yes`, and `1` disable model invocation, while `off`, `no`, and `0` leave commands available.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: bundle command loading excludes commands marked with `disable-model-invocation: on`, `yes`, and `1`, while preserving commands marked with `off`, `no`, and `0`.
- Current-head proof at `4c493488d6642643a32103d79edce3232a9fcbe8`: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/bundle-commands.test.ts` passed with 1 test file and 1 test.

target.title: fix(workspaces): reject raw file binding pointers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users reading workspace Markdown or CSV file bindings with a JSON pointer could receive the full raw file even when the pointer selected a missing non-root value.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Workspaces file-binding resolver now applies the same pointer contract at the raw-text owner boundary: omitted or root pointers return the file content, malformed pointers raise the existing invalid-binding error, and syntactically valid non-root pointers raise the existing not-found error. This covers the `.md` and `.csv` raw-text micro-cluster without changing JSON pointer handling, configuration, schema, storage schema, or provider behavior.

## User Impact

Workspace data reads for `file:<path>#<pointer>` now give a clear binding error for unsupported raw-text member lookups instead of treating a missing Markdown or CSV pointer as a successful full-file read.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Docker E2E resource-ceiling checks could keep accumulating an oversized stats JSONL sample line before rejecting it, letting a malformed or stalled stats writer consume unnecessary memory.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stats scanner now counts streamed sample-line bytes and rejects any single sample line over 1 MiB before JSON parsing. Normal newline-delimited Docker stats samples still stream through the same resource ceiling checks, including LF, CRLF, and standalone CR delimiters.

target.title: fix(admin-http-rpc): reject oversized declared request bodies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Admin HTTP RPC callers could send oversized JSON request bodies and lose the structured 413 response when the request exceeded the 1 MiB route limit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Admin HTTP RPC handler now rejects oversized declared `Content-Length` values before reading the body. For streamed overflow, it preserves the structured 413 response and closes the request immediately after that response has been handed to the operating system, so a sender that keeps transmitting cannot retain the request in flowing mode.

## User Impact

Operators and host tooling using `POST /api/v1/admin/rpc` get a clear HTTP 413 JSON response for oversized declared or streamed request bodies. Invalid oversized requests do not reach Gateway RPC dispatch, and continued chunked uploads are closed after the response.

## Evidence

- Current-head repair: at `efe8cbd64663006af0f138d5243bb779b7a4f4dd`, the streamed-overflow branch closes the request after the 413 response `finish` event instead of leaving the oversized upload in flowing mode.
- Current-head GitHub proof: `Real behavior proof` passed for `efe8cbd64663006af0f138d5243bb779b7a4f4dd` (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29592790433/job/87925748028), exercising the Admin HTTP RPC oversized-body behavior.
- Regression coverage: `extensions/admin-http-rpc/src/handler.test.ts` uses a real Node HTTP client that exceeds the limit, keeps writing, receives the structured 413, and observes the connection close.
- Diff scope: `gh pr diff 104552 --repo openclaw/openclaw --name-only` shows the current PR diff is limited to `extensions/admin-http-rpc/src/handler.ts` and `extensions/admin-http-rpc/src/handler.test.ts`.

AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed the Admin HTTP RPC route boundary, Node stream iterator contract, response-finish cleanup path, and ClawSweeper feedback before updating this PR.

The Control UI mock has limited curated chat state for design QA, so reviewers have to rely on ad hoc sessions when checking empty chat, longer transcripts, markdown rendering, code blocks, tables, warnings, and recoverable error copy.

This PR adds stable dev/mock-only fixture sessions to the Control UI mock server. The proposed fixtures cover a New session empty state, a coding session, a response-shape showcase, and a markdown showcase without changing production gateway or session APIs.

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text

$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
    "serve",
    "--apps-root",
    "/private/var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp/apps"
  ],
  "cwdEndsWith": true,
  "toolFilter": {
    "include": [
      "capsule.*",
      "vision_map.snapshot",
      "vision_map.list_apps",
      "vision_map.list_workflows",
      "vision_map.describe_workflow",
      "vision_map.describe",
      "vision_map.detect_state",
      "vision_map.list_actions",
      "vision_map.describe_action",
      "vision_map.perform_action",
      "vision_map.run_workflow",
      "vision_map.verify",
      "vision_map.repair_minimal",
      "vision_map.export_trace"
    ],
    "exclude": [
      "vision_map.click_at",
      "vision_map.type_text",
      "vision_map.press_key",
      "vision_map.scroll",
      "vision_map.init",
      "vision_map.apply_patch",
      "vision_map.add_control",
      "vision_map.commit_*",
      "vision_map.harvest_session"
    ]
  }
}
```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts
git diff --check
pnpm check:docs
codex review --base origin/main
```

Regression coverage added: `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` now covers a Codex-compatible bundle MCP config with a filtered server and a relative `./apps` data root.

Validation results:

```text
src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: 1 file passed, 8 tests passed
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: All matched files use the correct format
git diff --check: passed
pnpm check:docs: Docs formatting clean; markdownlint 0 errors; MDX check passed; i18n glossary passed; checked_internal_links=4554; broken_links=0
codex review --base origin/main: No actionable correctness issues were found
```

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime behavior change; docs now describe existing bundle MCP filter behavior.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

What is the highest-risk area? The docs could overstate which configured MCP fields bundle MCP entries support.

How is that risk mitigated? Existing runtime code already reads `toolFilter` from bundle-provided server config, existing runtime tests cover filtering behavior, and this PR adds loader coverage proving the bundle file path preserves the filter before runtime discovery.

## Current review state

AI-assisted: yes.

Next action: maintainer review.

target.title: docs(memory): align descriptors and docs with recursive memory/**/*.md
target.body:
## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. Agent `main`, local embedding provider, per-agent SQLite memory store at `~/.openclaw/memory/main.sqlite`. After-patch text proof imports the modified TypeScript modules directly from this branch via `node --import tsx` against working tree at HEAD `30f15f4e22`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Step 1 — drop a nested dated memory file under `memory/2026-05/` with a unique token:

```
cat > ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku/memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md <<'EOF'
Recursive memory search proof.
Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
EOF
```

Step 2 — reindex the live agent's memory store:

```
openclaw memory index
```

Step 3 — search for the unique token to prove the nested path was indexed and is retrievable:

```
openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
```

Step 4 — on the PR branch checkout (`30f15f4e22`), import the modified descriptor/help modules at runtime via `tsx` and print the after-patch strings to prove the new `memory/**/*.md` wording is observable from a real runtime call site (not just the diff):

```
node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs   # imports FIELD_HELP and buildPromptSection from this branch
```

**After-fix evidence**: Terminal output from the installed `openclaw 2026.5.20` runtime on the live workspace, plus runtime-imported after-patch strings from this branch (absolute paths redacted to `~`):

```
$ openclaw memory status
Memory Search (main)
Provider: local (requested: local)
Sources: memory
Extra paths: ~/.openclaw/shared-memory
Indexed: 105/105 files . 933 chunks
Workspace: ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku
By source:
  memory . 105/105 files . 933 chunks
```

```
$ openclaw memory index
[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU
Memory index updated (main).
```

```
$ openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU
0.812 memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md:1-9
    Recursive memory search proof.
    Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
    This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
    to verify that nested dated memory files are indexed and searchable
    by the runtime.

0.450 memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/smoke/2026-04-27.md:1-6
0.432 memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/pr-draft.md:1-32
```

After-patch text observed from this branch (HEAD `30f15f4e22`) by importing the modified modules at runtime:

```
$ node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs
=== schema.help.ts: FIELD_HELP['agents.defaults.memorySearch'] ===
Vector search over MEMORY.md and memory/**/*.md (per-agent overrides supported).

=== prompt-section.ts: buildPromptSection({ memory_search + memory_get }) ===

    Citations are disabled: do not mention file paths or line numbers in replies unless the user explicitly asks.

=== extensions/memory-core/index.ts (post-patch source lines) ===

```

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text
1231  1230  grew  packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts
TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

```text
TypeScript LOC ratchet: checked 4 changed production files.
Gateway client watchdog: 19 passed (19)
Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw Gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text
onDispatched calls: 1
Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

Repository and package gates:

```text
Gateway-client package build: passed, including generated declarations
Scoped lint: passed
Scoped formatting: passed for all 6 changed files
```

On the failed head, hosted `check-prod-types` and `check-test-types` both passed; the only primary code failure was the LOC ratchet, with `openclaw/ci-gate` failing as its aggregate. Updated hosted CI will rerun those lanes on the repaired head.

target.title: docs: respect configured Crabbox provider for agent tests

Related: #104485

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary Crabbox agent commands were forced onto Blacksmith Testbox even when an operator had selected another eligible provider through `CRABBOX_PROVIDER`. That made machine-local provider preferences ineffective and could also cause local-container execution to be described as remote/Testbox proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

Aligns the root policy and both Crabbox/testing skills on one provider-selection contract:

1. Source trust, platform, and proof requirements determine eligible providers.
2. An explicit eligible provider requested by the user wins.
3. Ordinary eligible wrapper calls omit `--provider`, allowing `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` to override the repository default.
4. With no user or environment preference, Blacksmith Testbox remains the repository fallback.

The same contract is applied to the root policy plus the Crabbox, testing, and PR-maintainer skills, so PR workflows cannot reintroduce mandatory Testbox routing. This restores the original goal of #104485 without weakening the sanitized-AWS/secretless-CI requirements for untrusted source. It is the maintained replacement because the original PR branch could not be updated. Original contributor: @hxy91819.

## User Impact

Operators can set a machine-local preference such as `CRABBOX_PROVIDER=local-container` without changing the shared skill. AWS or another eligible provider can be selected the same way. Task-specific user requests still take priority, while unsafe or platform-incompatible choices remain blocked.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.
- `check:changed` passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, attributions, extension export guards, duplicate coverage, dependency pins, and formatting. Its repository-wide Plugin SDK API baseline reports a hash mismatch; the exact baseline command reproduces the same mismatch on a clean detached `origin/main` snapshot, so this PR does not introduce it.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed.
- Earlier exact-head failures were deterministic regressions on the old `main` baseline and did not reference either memory-lancedb file. The current `main` repair at [`2c95bd2387c`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2c95bd2387cdcfab5b3736f3ab6d08a4ad23cb65) is included; fresh exact-head CI run [29386264145](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29386264145) passed with 46 checks green, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.

Remote Testbox delegation was unavailable because the installed Crabbox binary is 0.16.0 while the current flow requires 0.22.0 or newer. The proof above is secretless local execution, and GitHub CI remains the remote verification lane.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:


Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

## Summary

- Problem: new Control UI dashboard sessions without a label/displayName fall back to raw session keys, making multiple new chats hard to distinguish.
- Solution: add a Control UI fallback that renders unnamed dashboard sessions as their local creation time.
- What changed: gateway session rows now expose `sessionStartedAt`; Control UI uses it for dashboard-session display fallback, with `updatedAt` as a legacy fallback.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): no persisted labels are written, no rename UI was added, and explicit labels/display names still win.

## Motivation

## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text

- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

target.title: [codex] Fix Anthropic Vertex npm audit regression
target.body:
## Summary

- remove the `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk` runtime dependency from the shipped OpenClaw package
- replace it with a small local Anthropic Vertex client built on the existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `google-auth-library@10.6.2`
- update the lockfile so the npm package no longer pulls `google-auth-library@9 -> gaxios@6 -> uuid@9`

## Why

`openclaw@2026.5.2-beta.1` introduced a clean npm audit regression for consumers: `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk@0.16.0` depends on `google-auth-library@^9.4.2`, which resolves to `gaxios@6.7.1` and `uuid@9.0.1`. npm ignores dependency package `overrides`, so the published OpenClaw package still audited with two moderate findings even though the pnpm workspace override resolved `uuid` internally.

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`
- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/anthropic-vertex`
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts`
- `pnpm audit --prod --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- packed this branch with `npm pack`, installed the tarball into a fresh npm project, and verified `npm audit --omit=dev --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- tarball install dependency tree no longer contains `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`, `google-auth-library@9`, `gaxios@6`, or `uuid@9`

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
